slides.title: Session assertion
slides.subtitle: A short-lived, audience-bound assertion for a pairwise user identity
slides.notes: To get a signed-out Session, a personal agent signs a Session assertion. This example shows what goes into one, and why each part is there.

slides.title: Why an assertion
slides.statement: The agent asks for a Session **as itself**, for a user, without impersonating the human.
slides.notes: The assertion identifies the agent, refers to the user only through an identifier made for this one company, names the exact authorization server it is meant for, and expires quickly.

slides.title: Who takes part
slides.diagram:
flowchart LR M["Model"] subgraph HOST["Your host, trusted"] direction TB H["PAP host
builds the claims"] -- "resolve subject" --> P[("Pairwise ID store")] H -- "sign the claims" --> S["Reactor signer
holds the private key"] end subgraph CO["Company"] direction TB A["Authorization server
verifies, issues Session"] end HOST -- "compact assertion" --> CO HOST -. "policy, Session ready" .-> M
slides.caption: The subject and the key stay in the host; the model learns the policy and an opaque reference.
slides.notes: The model only asks for a Session. Inside your trusted host, the PAP host resolves the user's pairwise subject for this company from the pairwise ID store, builds the claims, and has the Reactor signer sign them without the private key ever leaving it. Only the compact assertion crosses to the company, whose authorization server verifies it and issues a signed-out Session. Off to the side, the model gets the lifetime, the bindings and an opaque Session reference, never the subject, the jti, the claims, the assertion or the key.

slides.title: How it flows

items.title: Resolve
items.detail: The pairwise subject for this company

items.title: Session
items.detail: A signed-out Session Token, named by the proof's key

slides.notes: The host resolves the subject, builds the claims and has them signed. The company checks the signature, that it is the audience, that the time window holds, and that it has never seen this jti. It answers with a signed-out Session Token. The assertion does not name the Session: the token request carries a DPoP proof signed with a new Session Key, and that key's thumbprint names the Session from then on.

slides.title: What each claim does

rows.label: sub
values: Two companies cannot correlate the user

rows.label: iat, exp
values: Bounds how long it is useful

slides.notes: Each claim limits the damage if an assertion escapes. The subject cannot be matched across companies, the audience pins it to one server, the lifetime is short, and the unique identifier lets the company refuse a second use.

slides.title: How the company checks it
slides.diagram:
flowchart LR
  S["Signature valid?"] -- "yes" --> U["aud is this server?"]
  U -- "yes" --> T["Within iat and exp?"]
  T -- "yes" --> J["jti never seen?"]
  J -- "yes" --> OK["Signed-out Session Token"]
  S -- "no" --> R["Refused"]
  U -- "no" --> R
  T -- "no" --> R
  J -- "no" --> R
slides.caption: Every check must pass; one failure and the assertion is worth nothing.
slides.notes: Read it left to right, as the company's authorization server does. First the signature must verify against the agent's key. Then the audience must be this server's issuer, as one string and nothing else, not even its token endpoint URL, so an assertion meant for another company is useless here. Then the time must fall between iat and exp, which keeps the window short. Last, the jti must be new, so a copied assertion is refused the second time. Only when every answer is yes does the company issue a signed-out Session Token.

slides.title: Run it yourself
slides.cta: The Pydantic AI and Agent Runtimes examples build real Session claims and return only their policy
slides.notes: The small example stops at safe assertion policy: a Reactor plugin contributes a SQLite pairwise store, and the tool reports lifetime and bindings. The Session lifecycle example sends the assertion in a real token request, with a DPoP proof by a new Session Key.
